entries.6827f6864c8ed2edacab045e454beb3ba8a4928c: <div sID="gen17051" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="64" osisID="Isa.64" sID="Isa.64"/> <div eID="gen17051" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17052" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen17053" type="x-p"/> This chapter goes on with that pathetic pleading prayer which the church offered up to God in the latter part of the foregoing chapter. They had argued from their covenant-relation to God and his interest and concern in them; now here, I. They pray that God would appear in some remarkable and surprising manner for them against his and their enemies, <reference osisRef="Isa.64.1-Isa.64.2">ver. 1, 2</reference>. II. They plead what God had formerly done, and was always ready to do, for his people, <reference osisRef="Isa.64.3-Isa.64.5">ver. 3-5</reference>. III. They confess themselves to be sinful and unworthy of God's favour, and that they had deserved the judgments they were now under, <reference osisRef="Isa.64.6-Isa.64.7">ver. 6, 7</reference>. IV. They refer themselves to the mercy of God as a Father, and submit themselves to his sovereignty, <reference osisRef="Isa.64.8">ver. 8</reference>. V. They represent the very deplorable condition they were in, and earnestly pray for the pardon of sin and the turning away of God's anger, <reference osisRef="Isa.64.9-Isa.64.12">ver. 9-12</reference>. And this was not only intended for the use of the captive Jews, but may serve for direction to the church in other times of distress, what to ask of God and how to plead with him. Are God's people at any time in affliction, in great affliction? Let them pray, let them thus pray.
entries.b54156c3f28842d03db298134c04e128761dc035: <div eID="gen17053" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen17052" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Prayer for the Divine Presence; Blessings Prepared for the Saints. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 706.)</title> <div sID="gen17054" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Oh that thou wouldest rend the heavens, that thou wouldest come down, that the mountains might flow down at thy presence, <hi type="super">2</hi> As <hi type="italic">when</hi> the melting fire burneth, the fire causeth the waters to boil, to make thy name known to thine adversaries, <hi type="italic">that</hi> the nations may tremble at thy presence! <hi type="super">3</hi> When thou didst terrible things <hi type="italic">which</hi> we looked not for, thou camest down, the mountains flowed down at thy presence. <hi type="super">4</hi> For since the beginning of the world <hi type="italic">men</hi> have not heard, nor perceived by the ear, neither hath the eye seen, O God, beside thee, <hi type="italic">what</hi> he hath prepared for him that waiteth for him. <hi type="super">5</hi> Thou meetest him that rejoiceth and worketh righteousness, <hi type="italic">those that</hi> remember thee in thy ways: behold, thou art wroth; for we have sinned: in those is continuance, and we shall be saved. <div eID="gen17054" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17055" type="x-p"/> Here, I. The petition is that God would appear wonderfully for them now, <reference osisRef="Isa.63.1-Isa.63.2">v. 1, 2</reference>. Their case was represented in the close of the foregoing chapter as very sad and very hard, and in this case it was time to cry, "Help, Lord; O that God would manifest his zeal and his strength!" They had prayed (<reference osisRef="Isa.63.15">ch. lxiii. 15</reference>) that God would <hi type="italic">look down from heaven;</hi> here they pray that he would come down to deliver them, as he had said, <reference osisRef="Exod.3.8">Exod. iii. 8</reference>. 1. They desire that God would in his providence manifest himself both to them and for them. When God works some extraordinary deliverance for his people he is said to <hi type="italic">shine forth,</hi> to show himself strong; so, here, they pray that he would <hi type="italic">rend the heavens and come down,</hi> as when he delivered David he is said to <hi type="italic">bow the heavens, and come down</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.18.9">Ps. xviii. 9</reference>), to display his power, and justice, and goodness, in an extraordinary manner, so that all may take notice of them and acknowledge them. This God's people desire and pray for, that they themselves having the satisfaction of seeing him though his way be in the sea, others may be made to see him when his way is in the clouds. This is applicable to the second coming of Christ, when <hi type="italic">the Lord himself shall descend from heaven with a shout. Come, Lord Jesus, come quickly.</hi> 2. They desire that he would vanquish all opposition and that it might be made to give way before him: <hi type="italic">That the mountains might flow down at thy presence,</hi> that the fire of thy wrath may burn so fiercely against thy enemies as even to dissolve the rockiest mountains and melt them down before it, as metal in the furnace, which is made liquid and cast into what shape the operator pleases; so <hi type="italic">the melting fire burns,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.63.2">v. 2</reference>. Let things be put into a ferment, in order to a glorious revolution in favour of the church: <hi type="italic">As the fire causes the waters to boil.</hi> There is an allusion here, some think, to the <hi type="italic">volcanoes,</hi> or burning mountains, which sometimes send forth such sulphureous streams as make the adjacent rivers and seas to boil, which, perhaps, are left as sensible intimations of the power of God's wrath and warning—pieces of the final conflagration. 3. They desire that this may tend very much to the glory and honour of God, <hi type="italic">may make his name known,</hi> not only to his friends (they knew it before, and trusted in his power), but to his adversaries likewise, that they may know it and <hi type="italic">tremble at his presence,</hi> and may say, with the men of Bethshemesh, <hi type="italic">Who is able to stand before this holy Lord God? Who knows the power of his anger?</hi> Note, Sooner or later God will make his name known to his adversaries and force those to <hi type="italic">tremble at his presence</hi> that would not come and worship in his presence. God's name, if it be not a stronghold for us, into which we may run and be safe, will be a strong-hold against us, out of the reach of which we cannot run and be safe. The day will come when nations shall be made to tremble at the presence of God, though they be ever so numerous and strong. <div eID="gen17055" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17056" type="x-p"/> II. The plea is that God had appeared wonderfully for his people formerly; and <hi type="italic">thou hast,</hi> therefore <hi type="italic">thou wilt,</hi> is good arguing at the throne of grace, <reference osisRef="Ps.10.17">Ps. x. 17</reference>. <div eID="gen17056" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17057" type="x-p"/> 1. They plead what he had done for his people Israel in particular when he brought them out of Egypt, <reference osisRef="Isa.63.3">v. 3</reference>. He then <hi type="italic">did terrible things</hi> in the plagues of Egypt, <hi type="italic">which they looked not for;</hi> they despaired of deliverance, so far were they from any thought of being delivered with such a high hand and outstretched arm. Then he came down upon Mount Sinai in such terror as made that and the adjacent mountains to <hi type="italic">flow down at his presence,</hi> to <hi type="italic">skip like rams</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.114.4">Ps. cxiv. 4</reference>), to tremble, so that they were scattered and the perpetual hills were made to bow, <reference osisRef="Hab.3.6">Hab. iii. 6</reference>. In the many great salvations God wrought for that people he did <hi type="italic">terrible things which they looked not for,</hi> made great men, that seemed as stately and strong as mountains, to fall before him, and great opposition to give way. See <reference osisRef="Judg.5.4-Judg.5.5">Judg. v. 4, 5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.68.7-Ps.68.8">Ps. lxviii. 7, 8</reference>. Some refer this to the defeat of Sennacherib's powerful army, which was as surprising an instance of the divine power as the melting down of rocks and mountains would be. <div eID="gen17057" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17058" type="x-p"/> 2. They plead what God had been used to do, and had declared his gracious purpose to do, for his people in general. The provision he has made for the safety and happiness of his people, even of all those that seek him, and serve him, and trust in him, is very rich and very ready, so that they need not fear being either disappointed of it, for it is sure, or disappointed in it, for it is sufficient. <div eID="gen17058" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17059" type="x-p"/> (1.) It is very rich, <reference osisRef="Isa.63.4">v. 4</reference>. Men have not heard nor seen what God has <hi type="italic">prepared for those that wait for him.</hi> Observe the character of God's people; they are such as wait for him in the way of duty, wait for the salvation he has promised and designed for them. Observe where the happiness of this people is bound up; it is <hi type="italic">what God has prepared for them,</hi> what he has designed for them in his counsel and is in his providence and grace preparing for them and preparing them for, what he has <hi type="italic">done</hi> or <hi type="italic">will</hi> do, so it may be read. Some of the Jewish doctors have understood this of the blessings reserved for the days of the Messiah, and to them the apostle applies these words; and others extend them to the glories of the world to come. It is all that goodness which God has <hi type="italic">laid up for those that fear him, and wrought for those that trust in him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.31.19">Ps. xxxi. 19</reference>. Of this it is here said that <hi type="italic">since the beginning of the world,</hi> in the most prying and inquisitive ages of it, men have not, either by hearing or seeing, the two learning senses, come to the full knowledge of it. None have seen, nor heard, nor can understand, but God himself, what the provision is that is made for the present and future felicity of holy souls. For, [1.] Much of it was concealed in former ages; they knew it not, because the <hi type="italic">unsearchable riches of Christ</hi> were <hi type="italic">hidden in God,</hi> were <hi type="italic">hidden from the wise and prudent;</hi> but in latter ages they were revealed by the gospel; so the apostle applies this (<reference osisRef="1Cor.2.9">1 Cor. ii. 9</reference>), for it follows (<reference osisRef="Isa.63.10">v. 10</reference>), <hi type="italic">But God has revealed them unto us by his Spirit;</hi> compare <reference osisRef="Rom.16.25">Rom. xvi. 25, 26, with</reference> <reference osisRef="Eph.3.9">Eph. iii. 9</reference>. That which men had not heard <hi type="italic">since the beginning of the world</hi> they should hear before the end of it, and at the end of it should see, when the veil shall be rent to introduce the glory that is yet to be revealed. God himself knew what he had in store for believers, but none knew besides him. [2.] It cannot be fully comprehended by the human understanding, no, not when it is revealed; it is spiritual, and refined from those ideas which our minds are most apt to receive in this world of sense; it is very great, and will far outdo the utmost of our expectations. Even the present peace of believers, much more their future bliss, is such as surpasses all conception and expression, <reference osisRef="Phil.4.7">Phil. iv. 7</reference>. None can comprehend it but God himself, whose understanding is infinite. Some give another reading of these words, referring the transcendency, not so much to the work itself as to the author of it: <hi type="italic">Neither has the eye seen a god besides thee, who doth so</hi> (or has done or can do so) <hi type="italic">for him that waits for him.</hi> We must infer from God's works of wonderous grace, as well as from his works of wondrous power, from the kind things, as well as from the great things, he does, that there is <hi type="italic">no god like him,</hi> nor any among the sons of the mighty to be compared with him. <div eID="gen17059" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17060" type="x-p"/> (2.) It is very ready (<reference osisRef="Isa.63.5">v. 5</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Thou meetest him that rejoices and works righteousness,</hi> meetest him with that good which thou hast prepared for him (<reference osisRef="Isa.63.4">v. 4</reference>), and dost not forget <hi type="italic">those that remember thee in thy ways.</hi>" See here what communion there is between a gracious God and a gracious soul. [1.] What God expects from us, in order to our having communion with him. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> We must make conscience of doing our duty in every thing, we must <hi type="italic">work righteousness,</hi> must do that which is good and which the Lord our God requires of us, and must do it well. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> We must be cheerful in doing our duty, we must <hi type="italic">rejoice and work righteousness,</hi> must delight ourselves in God and in his law, must be cheerful in his service and sing at our work. God loves a cheerful giver, a cheerful worshipper. We must <hi type="italic">serve the Lord with gladness. Thirdly,</hi> We must conform ourselves to all the methods of his providence concerning us and be suitably affected with them, must <hi type="italic">remember him in his ways,</hi> in all the ways wherein he walks, whether he walks towards us or walks contrary to us. We must mind him and make mention of him with thanksgiving when his ways are ways of mercy (<hi type="italic">in a day of prosperity be joyful</hi>), with patience and submission when he contends with us. <hi type="italic">In the way of thy judgments we have waited for thee;</hi> for <hi type="italic">in a day of adversity</hi> we must <hi type="italic">consider.</hi> [2.] We are here told what we may expect from God if we thus attend him in the way of duty: <hi type="italic">Thou meetest him.</hi> This intimates the friendship, fellowship, and familiarity to which God admits his people; he meets them, to converse with them, to manifest himself to them, and to receive their addresses, <reference osisRef="Exod.20.24">Exod. xx. 24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.29.43">xxix. 43</reference>. It likewise intimates his freeness and forwardness in doing them good; he will <hi type="italic">anticipate them with the blessings of his goodness,</hi> will <hi type="italic">rejoice to do good</hi> to those that <hi type="italic">rejoice in working righteousness,</hi> and wait to be gracious to those that <hi type="italic">wait for him.</hi> He meets his penitent people with a pardon, as the father of the prodigal met his returning son, <reference osisRef="Luke.15.20">Luke xv. 20</reference>. He meets his praying people with an answer of peace, while they are yet speaking, <reference osisRef="Isa.65.24">ch. lxv. 24</reference>. <div eID="gen17060" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17061" type="x-p"/> 3. They plead the unchangeableness of God's favour and the stability of his promise, notwithstanding the sins of his people and his displeasure against them for their sins: "<hi type="italic">Behold, thou hast</hi> many a time <hi type="italic">been wroth with us because we have sinned,</hi> and we have been under the tokens of thy wrath; <hi type="italic">but in those,</hi> those ways of thine, the ways of mercy in which we have <hi type="italic">remembered thee, in those is continuance,</hi>" or "<hi type="italic">in those thou art ever</hi>" (his mercy endures for ever), "<hi type="italic">and</hi> therefore <hi type="italic">we shall</hi> at last <hi type="italic">be saved,</hi> though thou art wroth, and we have sinned." This agrees with the tenour of God's covenant, that, if we <hi type="italic">forsake the law,</hi> he will <hi type="italic">visit our transgression with a rod,</hi> but <hi type="italic">his loving kindness</hi> he <hi type="italic">will not utterly take away, his covenant he will not break</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.89.30">Ps. lxxxix. 30</reference>, &c.), and by this his people have been many a time saved from ruin when they were just upon the brink of it; see <reference osisRef="Ps.78.38">Ps. lxxviii. 38</reference>. And by this continuance of the covenant we hope to be saved, for its being an everlasting covenant is all our salvation. Though God has been angry with us for our sins, and justly, yet his anger has endured but for a moment and has been soon over; but <hi type="italic">in his favour is life,</hi> because <hi type="italic">in it is continuance;</hi> in the ways of his favour he proceeds and perseveres, and on that we depend for our salvation, see <reference osisRef="Isa.54.7-Isa.54.8">ch. liv. 7, 8</reference>. It is well for us that our hopes of salvation are built not upon any merit or sufficiency of our own (for in that there is no certainty, even Adam in innocency did not abide), but upon God's mercies and promises, for <hi type="italic">in those,</hi> we are sure, <hi type="italic">is continuance.</hi>
entries.a9963464a090a7970b41f162c3115c90112739ff: <div eID="gen17061" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Humble Confession. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 706.)</title> <div sID="gen17062" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">6</hi> But we are all as an unclean <hi type="italic">thing,</hi> and all our righteousnesses <hi type="italic">are</hi> as filthy rags; and we all do fade as a leaf; and our iniquities, like the wind, have taken us away. <hi type="super">7</hi> And <hi type="italic">there is</hi> none that calleth upon thy name, that stirreth up himself to take hold of thee: for thou hast hid thy face from us, and hast consumed us, because of our iniquities. <hi type="super">8</hi> But now, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , thou <hi type="italic">art</hi> our father; we <hi type="italic">are</hi> the clay, and thou our potter; and we all <hi type="italic">are</hi> the work of thy hand. <hi type="super">9</hi> Be not wroth very sore, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , neither remember iniquity for ever: behold, see, we beseech thee, we <hi type="italic">are</hi> all thy people. <hi type="super">10</hi> Thy holy cities are a wilderness, Zion is a wilderness, Jerusalem a desolation. <hi type="super">11</hi> Our holy and our beautiful house, where our fathers praised thee, is burned up with fire: and all our pleasant things are laid waste. <hi type="super">12</hi> Wilt thou refrain thyself for these <hi type="italic">things,</hi> <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> ? wilt thou hold thy peace, and afflict us very sore? <div eID="gen17062" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17063" type="x-p"/> As we have the Lamentations of Jeremiah, so here we have the Lamentations of Isaiah; the subject of both is the same—the destruction of Jerusalem by the Chaldeans and the sin of Israel that brought that destruction—only with this difference, Isaiah sees it at a distance and laments it by the Spirit of prophecy, Jeremiah saw it accomplished. In these verses, <div eID="gen17063" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17064" type="x-p"/> I. The people of God in their affliction confess and bewail their sins, thereby justifying God in their afflictions, owning themselves unworthy of his mercy, and thereby both improving their troubles and preparing for deliverance. Now that they were under divine rebukes for sin they had nothing to trust to but the mere mercy of God and the continuance of that; for among themselves there is none to help, none to uphold, none to stand in the gap and make intercession, for they are all polluted with sin and therefore unworthy to intercede, all careless and remiss in duty and therefore unable and unfit to intercede. <div eID="gen17064" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17065" type="x-p"/> 1. There was a general corruption of manners among them (<reference osisRef="Isa.63.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">We are all as an unclean thing,</hi> or as an unclean <hi type="italic">person,</hi> as one overspread with a leprosy, who was to be shut out of the camp. The body of the people were like one under a ceremonial pollution, who was not admitted into the courts of the tabernacle, or like one labouring under some loathsome disease, from the crown of the head to the sole of the foot <hi type="italic">nothing but wounds and bruises,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.1.6">ch. i. 6</reference>. We have all by sin become not only obnoxious to God's justice, but odious to his holiness; for sin is that <hi type="italic">abominable thing which the Lord hates,</hi> and cannot endure to look upon. <hi type="italic">Even all our righteousnesses are as filthy rags.</hi> (1.) "The best of our persons are so; we are all so corrupt and polluted that even those among us who pass for righteous men, in comparison with what our fathers were who <hi type="italic">rejoiced and wrought righteousness</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.63.5">v. 5</reference>), are but as filthy rags, fit to be case to the dunghill. <hi type="italic">The best of them is as a brier.</hi>" (2.) "The best of our performances are so. There is not only a general corruption of manners, but a general defection in the exercises of devotion too; those which pass for the <hi type="italic">sacrifices of righteousness,</hi> when they come to be enquired into, are <hi type="italic">the torn, and the lame, and the sick,</hi> and therefore are provoking to God, as nauseous as filthy rags." Our performances, though they be ever so plausible, if we depend upon them as our righteousness and think to merit by them at God's hand, are as filthy rags—rags, and will not cover us—filthy rags, and will but defile us. True penitents cast away their idols as filthy rags (<reference osisRef="Isa.30.22">ch. xxx. 22</reference>), odious in their sight; here they acknowledge even their righteousness to be so in God's sight if he should deal with them in strict justice. Our best duties are so defective, and so far short of the rule, that they are as rags, and so full of sin and corruption cleaving to them that they are as filthy rags. When we would do good evil is present with us; and the iniquity of our holy things would be our ruin if we were under the law. <div eID="gen17065" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17066" type="x-p"/> 2. There was a general coldness of devotion among them, <reference osisRef="Isa.63.7">v. 7</reference>. The measure was filled by the abounding iniquity of the people, and nothing was done to empty it. (1.) Prayer was in a manner neglected: "<hi type="italic">There is none that calls on thy name,</hi> none that seeks to thee for grace to reform us and take away sin, or for mercy to relieve us and take away the judgments which our sins have brought upon us." <hi type="italic">Therefore</hi> people are so bad, because they do not pray; compare <reference osisRef="Ps.14.3-Ps.14.4">Ps. xiv. 3, 4</reference>, <hi type="italic">They have altogether become filthy, for they call not upon the Lord.</hi> It bodes ill to a people when prayer is restrained among them. (2.) It was very negligently performed. If there was here and there one that called on God's name, it was with a great deal of indifferency: <hi type="italic">There is none that stirs up himself to take hold of God.</hi> Note, [1.] To pray is to <hi type="italic">take hold of God,</hi> by faith to take hold of the promises and the declarations God has made of his good-will to us and to plead them with him,—to take hold of him as of one who is about to depart from us, earnestly begging of him not to leave us, or of one that has departed, soliciting his return,—to take hold of him as he that wrestles takes hold of him he wrestles with; for the seed of Jacob wrestle with him and so prevail. But when we <hi type="italic">take hold of God</hi> it is as the boatman with his hook takes hold on the shore, as if he would pull the shore to him, but really it is to pull himself to the shore; so we pray, not to bring God to our mind, but to bring ourselves to him. [2.] Those that would take hold of God in prayer so as to prevail with him must stir up themselves to do it; all that is within us must be employed in the duty (and all little enough), our thoughts fixed and our affections flaming. In order hereunto all that is within us must be engaged and summoned into the service; we must <hi type="italic">stir up the gift that is in us</hi> by an actual consideration of the importance of the work that is before us and a close application of mind to it; but how can we expect that God should come to us in ways of mercy when there are none that do this, when those that profess to be intercessors are mere triflers? <div eID="gen17066" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17067" type="x-p"/> II. They acknowledge their afflictions to be the fruit and product of their own sins and God's wrath. 1. They brought their troubles upon themselves by their own folly: "<hi type="italic">We are all as an unclean thing, and</hi> therefore <hi type="italic">we do all fade away as a leaf</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.63.6">v. 6</reference>), we not only wither and lose our beauty, but we fall and drop off" (so the word signifies) "as leaves in autumn; our profession of religion withers, and we grow dry and sapless; our prosperity withers and comes to nothing; we fall to the ground, as despicable and contemptible; and then <hi type="italic">our iniquities like the wind have taken us away</hi> and hurried us into captivity, as the winds in autumn blow off, and then blow away, the faded withered leaves," <reference osisRef="Ps.1.3-Ps.1.4">Ps. i. 3, 4</reference>. Sinners are blasted, and then carried away, by the malignant and violent wind of their own iniquity; it withers them and then ruins them. 2. God brought their troubles upon them by his wrath (<reference osisRef="Isa.63.7">v. 7</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thou hast hidden thy face from us;</hi> hast been displeased with us and refused to afford us any succour. When they made themselves <hi type="italic">as an unclean thing</hi> no wonder that God turned his face away from them, as loathing them. Yet this was not all: <hi type="italic">Thou hast consumed us because of our iniquities.</hi> This is the same complaint with that (<reference osisRef="Ps.90.7-Ps.90.8">Ps. xc. 7, 8</reference>), <hi type="italic">We are consumed by thy anger;</hi> thou hast <hi type="italic">melted us,</hi> so the word is. God had put them in the furnace, not to consume them as dross, but to melt them as gold, that they might be refined and new-cast. <div eID="gen17067" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17068" type="x-p"/> III. They claim relation to God as their God, and humbly plead it with him, and in consideration of it cheerfully refer themselves to him (<reference osisRef="Isa.63.8">v. 8</reference>): "<hi type="italic">But now, O Lord! thou art our Father:</hi> though we have conducted ourselves very undutifully and ungratefully towards thee, yet still we have owned thee as our Father; and, though thou hast corrected us, yet thou hast not cast us off. Foolish and careless as we are, poor and despised and trampled upon as we are by our enemies, yet still <hi type="italic">thou art our Father;</hi> to thee therefore we return in our repentance, as the prodigal arose and came to his father; to thee we address ourselves by prayer; from whom should we expect relief and succour but from our Father? It is the wrath of a Father that we are under, who will be reconciled and not <hi type="italic">keep his anger for ever.</hi>" God is their Father, 1. By creation; he gave them their being, formed them into a people, shaped them as he pleased: "<hi type="italic">We are the clay and thou our potter,</hi> therefore we will not quarrel with thee, however thou art pleased to deal with us, <reference osisRef="Jer.18.6">Jer. xviii. 6</reference>. Nay, therefore we will hope that thou wilt deal well with us, that thou who madest us wilt new-make us, new-form us, though we have unmade and deformed ourselves: <hi type="italic">We are all as an unclean thing,</hi> but <hi type="italic">we are all the work of thy hands,</hi> therefore do away our uncleanness, that we may be fit for thy use, the use we were made for. We are the <hi type="italic">work of thy hands,</hi> therefore <hi type="italic">forsake us not,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Ps.138.8">Ps. cxxxviii. 8</reference>. 2. By covenant; this is pleaded (<reference osisRef="Isa.63.9">v. 9</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Behold, see, we beseech thee, we are all thy people,</hi> all the people thou hast in the world, that make open profession of thy name. We are called <hi type="italic">thy people,</hi> our neighbours look upon us as such, and therefore what we suffer reflects upon thee, and the relief that our case requires is expected from thee. <hi type="italic">We are thy people;</hi> and <hi type="italic">should not a people seek unto their God?</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.8.19">ch. viii. 19</reference>. <hi type="italic">We are thine; save us,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Ps.119.94">Ps. cxix. 94</reference>. Note, When we are under providential rebukes from God it is good to keep fast hold of our covenant-relation to him. <div eID="gen17068" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17069" type="x-p"/> IV. They are importunate with God for the turning away of his anger and the pardoning of their sins (<reference osisRef="Isa.63.9">v. 9</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Be not wroth very sore, O Lord!</hi> though we have deserved that thou shouldst, <hi type="italic">neither remember iniquity for ever</hi> against us." They do not expressly pray for the removal of the judgment they were under; as to that, they refer themselves to God. But, 1. They pray that God would be reconciled to them, and then they can be easy whether the affliction be continued or removed: "<hi type="italic">Be not wroth to extremity,</hi> but let thy anger be mitigated by the clemency and compassion of a father." They do not say, <hi type="italic">Lord, rebuke us not,</hi> for that may be necessary, but <hi type="italic">Not in thy anger, not in thy hot displeasure.</hi> It is but <hi type="italic">in a little wrath</hi> that God <hi type="italic">hides his face.</hi> 2. They pray that they may not be dealt with according to the desert of their sin: <hi type="italic">Neither remember iniquity for ever.</hi> Such is the evil of sin that it deserves to be remembered for ever; and this is that which they deprecate, that consequence of sin, which is for ever. Those make it to appear that they are truly humbled under the hand of God who are more afraid of the terror of God's wrath, and the fatal consequences of their own sin, than of any judgment whatsoever, looking upon these as the sting of death. <div eID="gen17069" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17070" type="x-p"/> V. They lodge in the court of heaven a very melancholy representation, or memorial, of the lamentable condition they were in and the ruins they were groaning under. 1. Their own houses were in ruins, <reference osisRef="Isa.63.10">v. 10</reference>. The cities of Judah were destroyed by the Chaldeans and the inhabitants of them were carried away, so that there was none to repair them or take any notice of them, which would in a few years make them look like perfect deserts: <hi type="italic">Thy holy cities are a wilderness.</hi> The cities of Judah are called <hi type="italic">holy cities,</hi> for the people were unto God a kingdom of priests. The cities had synagogues in them, in which God was served; and therefore they lamented the ruins of them, and insisted upon this in pleading with God for them, not so much that they were stately cities, rich or ancient ones, but that they were holy cities, cities in which God's name was known, professed, and called upon. "These cities are a wilderness; the beauty of them is sullied; they are neither inhabited nor visited, as formerly. <hi type="italic">They have burnt up all the synagogues of God in the land,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Ps.74.8">Ps. lxxiv. 8</reference>. Nor was it only the smaller cities that were thus left as a wilderness unfrequented, but even "<hi type="italic">Zion is a wilderness;</hi> the city of David itself lies in ruins; Jerusalem, that was <hi type="italic">beautiful for situation</hi> and <hi type="italic">the joy of the whole earth,</hi> is now deformed, and has become the scorn and scandal of the whole earth; that noble city is a desolation, a heap of rubbish." See what devastations sin brings upon a people; and an external profession of sanctity will be no fence against them; <hi type="italic">holy cities,</hi> if they become wicked cities, will be soonest of all turned into a wilderness, <reference osisRef="Amos.3.2">Amos iii. 2</reference>. 2. God's house was in ruins, <reference osisRef="Isa.63.11">v. 11</reference>. This they lament most of all, that <hi type="italic">the temple was burnt with fire;</hi> but, as soon as it was built, they were told what their sin would bring it to. <reference osisRef="2Chr.7.21">2 Chron. vii. 21</reference>, <hi type="italic">This house, which is high, shall be an astonishment.</hi> Observe how pathetically they bewail the ruins of the temple. (1.) It was <hi type="italic">their holy and beautiful house;</hi> it was a most sumptuous building, but the holiness of it was in their eye the greatest beauty of it, and consequently the profanation of it was the saddest part of its desolation and that which grieved them most, that the sacred services which used to be performed there were discontinued. (2.) It was the place <hi type="italic">where their fathers praised God</hi> with their sacrifices and songs; what a pity is it that that should lie in ashes which had been for so many ages the glory of their nation! It aggravated their present disuse of the songs of Zion that their fathers had so often praised God with them. They interest God in the cause when they plead that it was the house where <hi type="italic">he had been praised,</hi> and put him in mind too of his covenant with their fathers by taking notice of their fathers' praising him. (3.) With it <hi type="italic">all their pleasant things were laid waste,</hi> all their desires and delights, all those things which were employed by them in the service of God, which they had a great delight in; not only the furniture of the temple, the altars and table, but especially the sabbaths and new moons, and all their religious feasts, which they used to keep with gladness, their ministers and solemn assemblies, these were all a desolation. Note, God's people reckon their sacred things their most delectable things; rob them of holy ordinances and the means of grace, and you <hi type="italic">lay waste all their pleasant things.</hi> What have they more? Observe here how God and his people have their interest twisted and interchanged; when they speak of the cities for their own habitation they call them <hi type="italic">thy holy cities,</hi> for to God they were dedicated; when they speak of the temple wherein God dwelt they call it <hi type="italic">our beautiful</hi> house and its furniture <hi type="italic">our pleasant things,</hi> for they had heartily espoused it and all the interests of it. If thus we interest God in all our concerns by devoting them to his service, and interest ourselves in all his concerns by laying them near our hearts, we may with satisfaction leave both with him, for he will perfect both. <div eID="gen17070" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17071" type="x-p"/> VI. They conclude with an affectionate expostulation, humbly arguing with God concerning their present desolations (<reference osisRef="Isa.64.12">v. 12</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Wilt thou refrain thyself for these things?</hi> Or, <hi type="italic">Canst thou contain thyself at these things?</hi> Canst thou see thy temple ruined and not resent it, not revenge it? Has the jealous God forgotten to be jealous? <reference osisRef="Ps.74.22">Ps. lxxiv. 22</reference>, <hi type="italic">Arise, O God! plead thy own cause.</hi> Lord, thou art insulted, thou art blasphemed; and <hi type="italic">wilt thou hold thy peace</hi> and take no notice of it? Shall the highest affronts that can be done to Heaven pass unrebuked?" When we are abused we hold our peace, because vengeance does not belong to us, and because we have a God to refer our cause to. When God is injured in his honour it may justly be expected that he should speak in the vindication of it; his people prescribe not to him what he shall say, but their prayer is (as here) <reference osisRef="Ps.83.1">Ps. lxxxiii. 1</reference>, <hi type="italic">Keep not thou silence, O God!</hi> and <reference osisRef="Ps.109.1">Ps. cix. 1</reference>, "<hi type="italic">Hold not thy peace, O God of my praise!</hi> Speak for the conviction of thy enemies, speak for the comfort and relief of thy people; for <hi type="italic">wilt thou afflict us very grievously,</hi> or <hi type="italic">afflict us for ever?</hi>" It is a sore affliction to good people to see God's sanctuary laid waste and nothing done towards the raising of it out of its ruins. But God has said that he <hi type="italic">will not contend for ever,</hi> and therefore his people may depend upon it that their afflictions shall be neither to extremity nor to eternity, but <hi type="italic">light</hi> and <hi type="italic">for a moment.</hi>  <chapter eID="Isa.64"/> <div eID="gen17071" type="x-p"/>

entries.c7ff1248265ce8f5351be2b78ed38fa309e98199: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9512"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 64</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Isa.64.1-Isa.64.12">Is 64:1-12</reference>. Transition from Complaint to Prayer.</title> <div sID="gen16605" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9512"/><hi type="bold">1. rend ... heavens--</hi>bursting forth to execute vengeance, suddenly descending on Thy people's foe (<reference osisRef="Ps.18.9">Psa 18:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.144.5">144:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hab.3.5">Ha 3:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Hab.3.6">6</reference>).<div eID="gen16605" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16606" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">flow down--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Judg.5.5">Jud 5:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.1.4">Mi 1:4</reference>). <div eID="gen16606" type="x-p"/>
entries.70f398e4ce45b45ea45eae116f2628114dc74fb7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9513"/><div sID="gen16607" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9513"/>2. Oh, that Thy wrath would consume Thy foes as the fire. Rather, "as the fire burneth the dry brushwood" [Gesenius]. <div eID="gen16607" type="x-p"/>
entries.6d89ec847c79da8775513462005a57ca066c1231: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9514"/><div sID="gen16608" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9514"/><hi type="bold">3. When--</hi>Supply from <reference osisRef="Isa.64.2">Is 64:2</reference>, "As when."<div eID="gen16608" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16609" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">terrible things--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.65.5">Psa 65:5</reference>).<div eID="gen16609" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16610" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">we looked not for--</hi>far exceeding the expectation of any of our nation; unparalleled before (<reference osisRef="Exod.34.10">Ex 34:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.68.8">Psa 68:8</reference>).<div eID="gen16610" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16611" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">camest down--</hi>on Mount Sinai.<div eID="gen16611" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16612" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">mountains flowed--</hi>Repeated from <reference osisRef="Isa.64.1">Is 64:1</reference>; they pray God to do the very same things for Israel now as in former ages. Gesenius, instead of "flowed" here, and "flow" in <reference osisRef="Isa.64.1">Is 64:1</reference>, translates from a different Hebrew root, "quake ... quaked"; but "fire" melts and causes to flow, rather than to quake (<reference osisRef="Isa.64.2">Is 64:2</reference>). <div eID="gen16612" type="x-p"/>
entries.f8b64185b7d5d65a31fecc7882b0af96880f300d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9515"/><div sID="gen16613" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9515"/><hi type="bold">4. perceived by the ear--</hi>Paul (<reference osisRef="1Cor.2.9">1Co 2:9</reference>) has for this, "nor have entered into the heart of man"; the virtual sense, sanctioned by his inspired authority; men might hear with the outward ear, but they could only by the Spirit "perceive" with the "heart" the spiritual significancy of God's acts, both those in relation to Israel, primarily referred to here, and those relating to the Gospel secondarily, which Paul refers to.<div eID="gen16613" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16614" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">O God ... what he ... prepared--</hi>rather, "nor hath eye seen a god beside thee who doeth such things." They refer to God's past marvellous acts in behalf of Israel as a plea for His now interposing for His people; but the Spirit, as Paul by inspiration shows, contemplated further God's revelation in the Gospel, which abounds in marvellous paradoxes never before heard of by carnal ear, not to be understood by mere human sagacity, and when foretold by the prophets not fully perceived or credited; and even after the manifestation of Christ not to be understood save through the inward teaching of the Holy Ghost. These are partly past and present, and partly future; therefore Paul substitutes "prepared" for "doeth," though his context shows he includes all three. For "waiteth" he has "love Him"; godly waiting on Him must flow from love, and not mere fear. <div eID="gen16614" type="x-p"/>
entries.9ea8f3c3f02087a646b630cb697a12d054fb3e13: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9516"/><div sID="gen16615" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9516"/><hi type="bold">5. meetest--</hi>that is, Thou makest peace, or enterest into covenant with him (see on <reference osisRef="Isa.47.3">Is 47:3</reference>).<div eID="gen16615" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16616" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">rejoiceth and worketh--</hi>that is, who with joyful willingness worketh [Gesenius] (<reference osisRef="Acts.10.35">Ac 10:35</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.7.17">Joh 7:17</reference>).<div eID="gen16616" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16617" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">those--</hi>Thou meetest "those," in apposition to "him" who represents a class whose characteristics "those that," &c., more fully describes.<div eID="gen16617" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16618" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">remember thee in thy ways--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.26.8">Is 26:8</reference>).<div eID="gen16618" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16619" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sinned--</hi>literally, "tripped," carrying on the figure in "ways."<div eID="gen16619" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16620" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in those is continuance--</hi>a plea to deprecate the continuance of God's wrath; it is not in Thy wrath that there is continuance (<reference osisRef="Isa.54.7">Is 54:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.54.8">8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.30.5">Psa 30:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.103.9">103:9</reference>), but in Thy ways ("those"), namely, of covenant mercy to Thy people (<reference osisRef="Mic.7.18-Mic.7.20">Mi 7:18-20</reference>; Mal 3:6); on the strength of the everlasting continuance of His covenant they infer by faith, "we shall be saved." God "remembered" for them His covenant (<reference osisRef="Ps.106.45">Psa 106:45</reference>), though they often "remembered not" Him (<reference osisRef="Ps.78.42">Psa 78:42</reference>). Castellio translates, "we have sinned for long in them ('thy ways'), and could we then be saved?" But they hardly would use such a plea when their very object was to be saved. <div eID="gen16620" type="x-p"/>
entries.27bb5f7091e457ed2ca88d93d1223064a3a96f34: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9517"/><div sID="gen16621" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9517"/><hi type="bold">6. unclean thing--</hi>legally unclean, as a leper. True of Israel, everywhere now cut off by unbelief and by God's judgments from the congregation of the saints.<div eID="gen16621" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16622" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">righteousness--</hi>plural, "uncleanness" extended to every particular act of theirs, even to their prayers and praises. True of the best doings of the unregenerate (<reference osisRef="Phil.3.6-Phil.3.8">Php 3:6-8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Titus.1.15">Tit 1:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.11.6">He 11:6</reference>).<div eID="gen16622" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16623" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">filthy rags--</hi>literally, a "menstruous rag" (<reference osisRef="Lev.15.33">Le 15:33</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.20.18">20:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lam.1.17">La 1:17</reference>).<div eID="gen16623" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16624" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fade ... leaf--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.90.5">Psa 90:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.90.6">6</reference>). <div eID="gen16624" type="x-p"/>
entries.81c7a75fdb53beaee3317ed4f3691ef083ed7797: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9518"/><div sID="gen16625" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9518"/><hi type="bold">7. stirreth--</hi>rouseth himself from spiritual drowsiness.<div eID="gen16625" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16626" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">take hold--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.27.5">Is 27:5</reference>). <div eID="gen16626" type="x-p"/>
entries.ecbd06a1d3ed631ecd02823272d45788f4afdfc1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9519"/><div sID="gen16627" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9519"/><hi type="bold">8. father--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.63.16">Is 63:16</reference>).<div eID="gen16627" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16628" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">clay ... potter--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.29.16">Is 29:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.45.9">45:9</reference>). Unable to mould themselves aright, they beg the sovereign will of God to mould them unto salvation, even as He made them at the first, and is their "Father." <div eID="gen16628" type="x-p"/>
entries.3e0b6f4bfab2698ca13ee0f687309d42ad2b2d53: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9520"/><div sID="gen16629" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9520"/>9. (<reference osisRef="Ps.74.1">Psa 74:1</reference>, 2).<div eID="gen16629" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16630" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">we are ... thy people--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jer.14.9">Jr 14:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.14.21">21</reference>). <div eID="gen16630" type="x-p"/>
entries.06d638bf74073259702f83cdc86b48338bbdd521: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9521"/><div sID="gen16631" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9521"/><hi type="bold">10. holy cities--</hi>No city but Jerusalem is called "the holy city" (<reference osisRef="Isa.48.2">Is 48:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.52.1">52:1</reference>); the plural, therefore, refers to the upper and the lower parts of the same city Jerusalem [Vitringa]; or all Judea was holy to God, so its cities were deemed "holy" [Maurer]. But the parallelism favors Vitringa. Zion and Jerusalem (the one city) answering to "holy cities." <div eID="gen16631" type="x-p"/>
entries.7a9abe231002f36a3562cd1c5bad233622dc7f4d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9522"/><div sID="gen16632" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9522"/><hi type="bold">11. house--</hi>the temple.<div eID="gen16632" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16633" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">beautiful--</hi>includes the idea of glorious (<reference osisRef="Mark.13.1">Mr 13:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.3.2">Ac 3:2</reference>).<div eID="gen16633" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16634" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">burned--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.74.7">Psa 74:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lam.2.7">La 2:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.36.19">2Ch 36:19</reference>). Its destruction under Nebuchadnezzar prefigured that under Titus.<div eID="gen16634" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16635" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">pleasant things--</hi>Hebrew, "objects of desire"; our homes, our city, and all its dear associations. <div eID="gen16635" type="x-p"/>
entries.b06bd8b19fd8e348f2b2d76babd764902c859f08: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9523"/><div sID="gen16636" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9523"/><hi type="bold">12. for these things--</hi>Wilt Thou, notwithstanding these calamities of Thy people, still refuse Thy aid (<reference osisRef="Isa.42.14">Is 42:14</reference>)? <chapter eID="Isa.64"/>

entries.b999bbd749087042508e23e76d7b6837e519f18a: <div eID="gen28999" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen29000" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen29001" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen29001" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen29000" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen29002" type="x-p"/> The whole of this chapter, which is very pathetic and tender, may be considered as a formulary of prayer and humiliation intended for the Jews in order to their conversion, <reference osisRef="Isa.64.1-Isa.64.12">Isa 64:1-12</reference>. <div eID="gen29002" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29003" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen29003" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29004" type="x-p"/> O that thou wouldest rend the heavens - This seems to allude to the wonderful manifestation of God upon Mount Sinai.
entries.e00c105756f1fbd7861cf49e1bec519815ab7316: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen29004" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29005" type="x-p"/> As when the melting fire burneth "As the fire kindleth the dry fuel" - המסים hamasim. "It means dry stubble, and the root is המס hamas, "says Rabbi Jonah, apud Sal ben Belec in loc. Which is approved by Schultens, Orig. Hebrews p. 30. "The fire kindling the stubble does not seem like enough to the melting of the mountains to be brought as a simile to it. What if thus? - 'That the mountains might flow down at thy presence! <div eID="gen29005" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29006" type="x-p"/> As the fire of things smelted burneth, <div eID="gen29006" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29007" type="x-p"/> As the fire causeth the waters to boil - ' <div eID="gen29007" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29008" type="x-p"/> There is no doubt of the Hebrew words of the second line bearing that version." - Dr. Jubb. <div eID="gen29008" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29009" type="x-p"/> I submit these different interpretations to the reader's judgment. For my own part I am inclined to think that the text is much corrupted in this place. The ancient Versions have not the least traces of either of the above interpretations. The Septuagint and Syriac agree exactly together in rendering this line by, "As the wax melted before the fire," which can by no means be reconciled with the present text. The Vulgate, for המסים hamasim, read ימסו yemasu. <div eID="gen29009" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29010" type="x-p"/> That the nations - For גוים goyim, the nations, four MSS. (one of them ancient) have הרים harim, the mountains. - L.
entries.023036f3ec0d0a4565fff3b8f207bb0e19326d30: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen29010" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29011" type="x-p"/> For since the beginning of the world men have not heard "For never have men heard" - St. Paul is generally supposed to have quoted this passage of Isaiah, <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.9">1Cor 2:9</reference>; and Clemens Romanus in his first epistle has made the same quotation, very nearly in the same words with the apostle. But the citation is so very different both from the Hebrew text and the version of the Septuagint, that it seems very difficult, if not impossible, to reconcile them by any literal emendation, without going beyond the bounds of temperate criticism. One clause, "neither hath it entered into the heart of man," (which, by the way, is a phrase purely Hebrew, עלה על לב alah al leb, and should seem to belong to the prophet), is wholly left out; and another is repeated without force or propriety; viz., "nor perceived by the ear," after, "never have heard:" and the sense and expression of the apostle is far preferable to that of the Hebrew text. Under these difficulties I am at a loss what to do better, than to offer to the reader this, perhaps disagreeable, alternative: either to consider the Hebrew text and Septuagint in this place as wilfully disguised and corrupted by the Jews; of which practice in regard to other quotations in the New Testament from the Old, they lie under strong suspicions, (see Dr. Owen on the version of the Septuagint, sect. vi.-ix.); or to look upon St. Paul's quotation as not made from Isaiah, but from one or other of the two apocryphal books, entitled, The Ascension of Esaiah, and the Apocalypse of Elias, in both of which this passage was found; and the apostle is by some supposed in other places to have quoted such apocryphal writings. As the first of these conclusions will perhaps not easily be admitted by many, so I must fairly warn my readers that the second is treated by Jerome as little better than heresy. See his comment on this place of Isaiah. - L. I would read the whole verse thus; "Yea, from the time of old they have not heard, they have not hearkened to, an eye hath not seen a God besides thee. He shall work for that one that waiteth for him." This I really think on the whole to be the best translation of the original. <div eID="gen29011" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29012" type="x-p"/> The variations on this place are as follows: for שמעו shameu, they have heard, a MS. and the Septuagint read שמענו shamanu, we have heard: for the second לא lo, not, sixty-nine MSS. and four editions have ולא velo, and not, and the Syriac, Chaldee, and Vulgate. And so ועין veayin, and eye, Septuagint and Syriac. את eth, the, (emphatic), is added before אלהים Elohim, God, in MS. Bodleian. למחכי limechakkey, to them that wait, plural, two MSS. and all the ancient Versions. - L.
entries.4b744666396a5ca5bda7adafabc06fbd1e4ca111: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen29012" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29013" type="x-p"/> Thou meetest him that rejoiceth and worketh righteousness "Thou meetest with joy those who work righteousness" - The Syriac reads פוגע אתה שש בעשי poga attah shesh baashi, as above. <div eID="gen29013" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29014" type="x-p"/> In those is continuance, and we shall be saved "Because of our deeds, for we have been rebellious" - בהם עולם ונושע bahem olam venivvashea. I am fully persuaded that these words as they stand in the present Hebrew text are utterly unintelligible; there is no doubt of the meaning of each word separately; but put together they make no sense at all. I conclude, therefore, that the copy has suffered by mistakes of transcribers in this place. The corruption is of long standing, for the ancient interpreters were as much at a loss for the meaning as the moderns, and give nothing satisfactory. The Septuagint render these words by δια τουτο επλανηθημεν, therefore we have erred: they seem to have read עליהם נפשע aleyhem niphsha, without helping the sense. In this difficulty what remains but to have recourse to conjecture? Archbishop Secker was dissatisfied with the present reading: he proposed הבט עלינו ונושע hebet aleynu venivvashea; "look upon us, and we shall, or that we may, be saved:" which gives a very good sense, but seems to have no sufficient foundation. Besides, the word ונושע venivvashea, which is attended with great difficulties, seems to be corrupted as well as the two preceding; and the true reading of it is, I think, given by the Septuagint, ונפשע veniphsha, επλανηθημεν, we have erred, (so they render the verb פשע pasha, <reference osisRef="Isa.46.8">Isa 46:8</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Eze.23.12">Eze 23:12</reference>), parallel to ונחטא vannecheta, ἡμαρτομεν, we have sinned. For בהם עולם bahem olam, which means nothing, I would propose המעללינו hammaaleleynu, "because of our deeds;" which I presume was first altered to במעלליהם bemaaleleyhem, an easy and common mistake of the third person plural of the pronoun for the first, (see note on <reference osisRef="Isa.33.2">Isa 33:2</reference>), and then with some farther alteration to בהם עולם behem olam. The עליהם aleyhem, which the Septuagint probably found in their copy, seems to be a remnant of במעלליהם bemaaleleyhem. <div eID="gen29014" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29015" type="x-p"/> This, it may be said, is imposing your sense upon the prophet. It may be so; for perhaps these may not be the very words of the prophet: but however it is better than to impose upon him what makes no sense at all; as they generally do, who pretend to render such corrupted passages. For instance, our own translators:" in those is continuance, and we shall be saved:" in those in whom, or what? There is no antecedent to the relative. "In the ways of God," say some: "with our fathers," says Vitringa, joining it in construction with the verb, קעפת katsaphta, "thou hast been angry with them, our fathers;" and putting ונחטא vannecheta, "for we have sinned," in a parenthesis. But there has not been any mention of our fathers: and the whole sentence, thus disposed, is utterly discordant from the Hebrew idiom and construction. In those is continuance; עולם olam means a destined but hidden and unknown portion of time; but cannot mean continuation of time, or continuance, as it is here rendered. Such forced interpretations are equally conjectural with the boldest critical emendation; and generally have this farther disadvantage, that they are altogether unworthy of the sacred writers. - L. <div eID="gen29015" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29016" type="x-p"/> Coverdale renders the passage thus: - <div eID="gen29016" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29017" type="x-p"/> But lo, thou art angrie, for we offende, and have been ever in synne; and there is not one whole. <div eID="gen29017" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29018" type="x-p"/> This is, I am afraid, making a sense. <div eID="gen29018" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29019" type="x-p"/> After all that this very learned prelate has done to reduce these words to sense and meaning, I am afraid we are still far from the prophet's mind. Probably בהם bahem, in them, refers to דרכיך deracheycha, thy ways, above. עולם olam may be rendered of old, or during the whole of the Jewish economy; and ונושע venivvashea, "and shall we be saved?" Thus: - Thou art wroth, for we have sinned in them (thy ways) of old; and can we be saved? For we are all as an unclean thing, etc.
entries.2f3a641a91143aca40c9171f9bf74a6ef314c83a: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen29019" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29020" type="x-p"/> As filthy rags - עדים iddim. Rab. Mosheh ben Maimon interpretatur עדים iddim, vestes quibus mulier se abstergit post congressum cum marito suo. Alii pannus menstruatus. Alii panni mulieris parientis. - And we ben made as unclene alle we: and as the cloth of the woman rooten blode flowing, all our rigtwisnesses. - Old MS. Bible. If preachers knew properly the meaning of this word, would they make such a liberal use of it in their public ministry? And why should any use a word, the meaning of which he does not understand? How many in the congregation blush for the incautious man and his "filthy rags!"
entries.6bec37254e4bc40f92c740ee70981bce0125c9f0: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen29020" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29021" type="x-p"/> There is none - Twelve MSS. have אין ein, without the conjunction ו vau prefixed; and so read the Chaldee and Vulgate. <div eID="gen29021" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29022" type="x-p"/> And hast consumed us because of our iniquities "And hast delivered us up into the hands of our iniquities" - For ותמוגנו vattemugenu, "hast dissolved us," the Septuagint, Syriac, and Chaldee had in their copies תמגננו temaggenenu, "hast delivered us up." Houbigant. Secker.
entries.6cafe715fb096c925aa7c099c8fe8a3cb5602617: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen29022" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29023" type="x-p"/> But, now, O Lord, thou art our Father "But thou, O Jehovah, thou art our Father" - For ועתה veattah, and now, five MSS., one of them ancient, and the two oldest editions, 1486 and 1488, have ואתה veattah, and thou, and so the Chaldee seems to have read. The repetition has great force. The other word may be well spared. "But now, O Lord, thou art our Father." How very affectionate is the complaint in this and the following verses! But how does the distress increase, when they recollect the desolations of the temple, and ruin of public worship, <reference osisRef="Isa.64.11">Isa 64:11</reference> : "Our holy and beautiful house, where our fathers praised thee, is burnt up with fire," etc. <div eID="gen29023" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29024" type="x-p"/> We all are the work of thy hand - Three MSS. (two of them ancient) and the Septuagint read מעשה maaseh, the work, without the conjunction ו vau prefixed. And for ידך yadecha, thy hand, the Bodleian, and two others MSS., the Septuagint, Syriac, and Vulgate read ידיך yadeycha, thy hands, in the plural number. - L.
entries.837a99533e3b0dc6560bcc42523d8ad8776ee825: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen29024" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29025" type="x-p"/> Neither remember iniquity - For לעד תזכר laad tizcor, one of my MSS. has לעד תקצף laad tiktsoph, "be not angry," as in the preceding clause. This has been partially obliterated, and תזכר tizcor, written in the margin by a later hand: but this MS. abounds with words of this kind, all altered by later hands.  <chapter eID="Isa.64"/> <div eID="gen29025" type="x-p"/>

entries.1129fd1c7da3d5d7af08934d9bada72edad14577: <reference osisRef="Isa.64.1-Isa.64.2">Isa 64:1-2</reference> <div eID="gen13664" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13665" type="x-p"/> The similes which follow cannot be attached to this <hi type="italic">nâzōllū</hi>, however we may explain it. Yet <reference osisRef="Isa.64.1">Isa 64:1</reference> (<reference osisRef="Isa.64.2">2</reference>) does not form a new and independent sentence; but we must in thought repeat the word upon which the principal emphasis rests in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Isa.63.19">Isa 63:19</reference></hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.64.1">Isa 64:1</reference>). “(<hi type="italic">Wouldst come down</hi>) <hi type="italic">as fire kindles brushwood, fire causes water to boil; to make known Thy name to Thine adversaries, that the heathen may tremble before Thy face! When Thou doest terrible things which we hoped not for; wouldst come down, </hi>(<hi type="italic">and</hi>)<hi type="italic">mountains shake before Thy countenance!</hi>” The older expositors gave themselves a great deal of trouble in the attempt to trace <hi type="italic">hămâsı̄m</hi> to <hi type="italic">mâsas</hi>, to melt. But since Louis de Dieu and Albert Schultens have followed Saadia and Abulwâlid in citing the Arabic <hi type="italic">hms</hi>, to crack, to mutter, to mumble, etc., and <hi type="italic">hšm</hi>, to break in pieces, <hi type="italic">confringere</hi>, from which comes <hi type="italic">hashim</hi>, broken, dry wood, it is generally admitted that <hi type="italic">hămâsim</hi> is from <hi type="italic">hemes</hi> (lit. crackling, rattling, Arab. <hi type="italic">hams</hi>), and signifies “dry twigs,” <hi type="italic">arida sarmenta</hi>. The second simile might be rendered, “as water bubbles up in the fire;” and in that case <hi type="italic">mayim</hi> would be treated as a feminine (according to the rule in Ges. §146, 3), in support of which <reference osisRef="Job.14.19">Job 14:19</reference> may be adduced as an unquestionable example (although in other cases it is masculine), and אשׁ = בּאשׁ would be used in a local sense, like <hi type="italic">lehâbhâh</hi>, into flames, in Isa 5:24. But it is much more natural to take אשׁ, which is just as often a feminine as מים is a masculine, as the subject of תּבעה, and to give to the verb בּעה, which is originally intransitive, judging from the Arabic <hi type="italic">bgâ</hi>, to swell, the Chald. בּוּע, to spring up (compare אבעבּעות, blisters, pustules), the Syr. בּגא, to bubble up, etc., the transitive meaning to cause to boil or bubble up, rather than the intransitive to boil (comp. <reference osisRef="Isa.30.13">Isa 30:13</reference>, נבעה, swollen = bent forwards, as it were <hi type="italic">protumidus</hi>). Jehovah is to come down with the same irresistible force which fire exerts upon brushwood or water, when it sets the former in flames and makes the latter boil; in order that by such a display of might He may make His name known (viz., the name thus judicially revealing itself, hence “in fire,” <reference osisRef="Isa.30.27">Isa 30:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.66.15">Isa 66:15</reference>) to His adversaries, and that nations (viz., those that are idolaters) may tremble before Him (מפּניך: cf., <reference osisRef="Ps.68.2-Ps.68.3">Psa 68:2-3</reference>). The infinitive clause denoting the purpose, like that indicating the comparison, passes into the finite (cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.10.2">Isa 10:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.13.9">Isa 13:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.14.25">Isa 14:25</reference>). Modern commentators for the most part now regard the optative <hi type="italic">lū'</hi> (O that) as extending to <reference osisRef="Isa.64.2">Isa 64:2</reference> also; and, in fact, although this continued influence of <hi type="italic">lū'</hi> appears to overstep the bounds of the possible, we are forced to resort to this extremity. <reference osisRef="Isa.64.2">Isa 64:2</reference> cannot contain a historical retrospect: the word “formerly” would be introduced if it did, and the order of the words would be a different one. Again, we cannot assume that נזלּוּ הרים מפּניך ירדתּ contains an expression of confidence, or that the prefects indicate certainty. Neither the context, the foregoing נוראות בּעשׂותך נו (why not עשׂה?), nor the parenthetical assertion נקוּה לא, permits of this. On the other hand, וגו בעשׂותך connects itself very appropriately with the purposes indicated in <reference osisRef="Isa.64.1">Isa 64:1</reference> (2.): “may tremble when Thou doest terrible things, which we, i.e., such as we, do not look for,” i.e., which surpass our expectations. And now nothing remains but to recognise the resumption of <reference osisRef="Isa.63.19">Isa 63:19</reference> (<reference osisRef="Isa.64.1">Isa 64:1</reference>) in the clause “The mountains shake at Thy presence,” in which case Isaiah 63:19 <hi type="italic">b</hi>-64:2 (<reference osisRef="Isa.64.1-Isa.64.3">Isa 64:1-3</reference>) forms a grand period rounded off palindromically after Isaiah’s peculiar style.
entries.08b9ff98e2a7b83bd37b6fd586dc6a943a745114: <reference osisRef="Isa.64.3">Isa 64:3</reference> <div eID="gen13665" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13666" type="x-p"/> The following clause gives the reason for this; ו being very frequently the logical equivalent for <hi type="italic">kı̄</hi> (e.g., <reference osisRef="Isa.3.7">Isa 3:7</reference> and <reference osisRef="Isa.38.15">Isa 38:15</reference>). The justification of this wish, which is forced from them by the existing misery, is found in the incomparable acts of Jehovah for the good of His own people, which are to be seen in a long series of historical events. <reference osisRef="Isa.64.3">Isa 64:3</reference> (4.). <hi type="italic">“For from olden time men have not heard, nor perceived, nor hath an eye seen, a God beside Thee, who acted on behalf of him that waiteth for Him.”</hi> No ear, no eye has ever been able to perceive the existence of a God who acted like Jehovah, i.e., really interposed on behalf of those who set their hopes upon Him. This is the explanation adopted by Knobel; but he wrongly supplies נוראות to יעשׂה, whereas עשׂה is used here in the same pregnant sense as in Ps. 22:32; <reference osisRef="Ps.37.5">Psa 37:5</reference>; 52:11 (cf., <hi type="italic">gâmar</hi> in <reference osisRef="Ps.57.3">Psa 57:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.138.8">Psa 138:8</reference>). It has been objected to this explanation, that האזין is never connected with the accusative of the person, and that God can neither be heard nor seen. But what is terrible in relation to שׁמע in <reference osisRef="Job.42.5">Job 42:5</reference> cannot be untenable in relation to האזין. Hearing and seeing God are here equivalent to recognising His existence through the perception of His works. The explanation favoured by Rosenmüller and Stier, viz., “And from olden time men have not heard it, nor perceived with ears, no eye has seen it, O God, beside Thee, what (this God) doth to him that waiteth for Him,” is open to still graver objections. The thought is the same as in <reference osisRef="Ps.31.20">Psa 31:20</reference>, and when so explained it corresponds more exactly to the free quotation in <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.9">1Co 2:9</reference>, which with our explanation there is no necessity to trace back to either <reference osisRef="Isa.42.15-Isa.42.16">Isa 42:15-16</reference>, or a lost book, as Origen imagined (see Tischendorf’s ed. vii. of the N.T. on this passage). This which no ear has heard, no eye seen, is not God Himself, but He who acts for His people, and justifies their waiting for Him (cf., Hofmann, <hi type="italic">Die h. Schrift Neuen Testaments</hi>, ii. 2, 51). Another proof that Paul had no other passage than this in his mind, is the fact that the same quotation is met with in Clement’s <hi type="italic">Epistle to the Corinthians</hi> (ch. 34), where, instead of “those that love Him,” we have “those that wait for Him,” a literal rendering of למחכּה־לו. The quotation by Paul therefore by no means leads us to take <hi type="italic">Elohim</hi> as a vocative or וגו יעשׂה as the object, although it must not be concealed that this view of the passage and its reference to the fulness of glory in the eternal life is an old rabbinical one, as Rashi expressly affirms, when he appeals to R. Jose (Joseph Kara) as bondsman for the other (see <hi type="italic">b. Sanhedrin </hi>99 <hi type="italic">a</hi>). Hahn has justly objected to this traditional explanation, which regards Elohim as a vocative, that the thought, that God alone has heard and perceived and seen with His eye what He intends to do to His people, is unsuitable in itself, and at variance with the context, and that if וגו יעשׂה was intended as the object, אשר (את) would certainly be inserted. And to this we may add, that we cannot find the words <hi type="italic">Elohim</hi> <hi type="italic">zūlâthekhâ</hi> (God beside Thee) preceded by a negation anywhere in chapters 40-66 without receiving at once the impression, that they affirm the sole deity of Jehovah (comp. <reference osisRef="Isa.45.5">Isa 45:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.45.21">Isa 45:21</reference>). The meaning therefore is, <hi type="italic">“No other God beside Jehovah has ever been heard or seen, who acted for </hi>(<hi type="italic">ageret pro</hi>)<hi type="italic">those who waited for Him.”</hi> <hi type="italic">Mechakkēh</hi> is the construct, according to Ges. §116, 1; and <hi type="italic">ya‛ăsēh</hi> has <hi type="italic">tsere</hi> here, according to Kimchi (<hi type="italic">Michlol</hi> 125 <hi type="italic">b</hi>) and other testimonies, just as we meet with תעסה four times (in <reference osisRef="Gen.26.29">Gen 26:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.7.9">Jos 7:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.13.12">2Sa 13:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.40.16">Jer 40:16</reference>) and ונעשׂה once (<reference osisRef="Josh.9.24">Jos 9:24</reference>), mostly with a disjunctive accent, and not without the influence of a whole or half pause, the form with <hi type="italic">tsere</hi> being regarded as more emphatic than that with <hi type="italic">seghol</hi>.<note placement="foot">In addition to the examples given above, we have the following forms of the same kind in kal: ימּצה (with <hi type="italic">tiphchah</hi>) in <reference osisRef="Jer.17.17">Jer 17:17</reference>; תּראה (with <hi type="italic">tsakpeh</hi>) in <reference osisRef="Dan.1.13">Dan 1:13</reference>, compare תּגלּה (with <hi type="italic">athnach</hi>) in <reference osisRef="Lev.18.7-Lev.18.8">Lev 18:7-8</reference>, and תגלּה (with the smaller disjunctive <hi type="italic">tiphchah</hi>) in <reference osisRef="Lev.18.9-Lev.18.11">Lev 18:9-11</reference>; ינקּה (with <hi type="italic">athnach</hi>) in <reference osisRef="Nah.1.3">Nah 1:3</reference>; אזרה (with <hi type="italic">tsakeph</hi>) in Eze 5:12. This influence of the accentuation has escaped the notice of the more modern grammarians (e.g., Ges. §75, Anm. 17).</note>
entries.17e3f5513a89fcfa03b4c610fc2968223e7b44dd: <reference osisRef="Isa.64.4">Isa 64:4</reference> <div eID="gen13666" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13667" type="x-p"/> After the long period governed by לוּא has thus been followed by the retrospect in <reference osisRef="Isa.64.3">Isa 64:3</reference> (4.), it is absolutely impossible that <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Isa.64.4">Isa 64:4</reference></hi> (5 <hi type="italic">a</hi>) should be intended as an optative, in the sense of “O that thou wouldst receive him that,” etc., as Stier and others propose. The retrospect is still continued thus: <hi type="italic">“Thou didst meet him that rejoiceth to work righteousness, when they remembered Thee in Thy ways.”</hi> צדק ועשׂה שׂשׂ is one in whom joy and right action are paired, and is therefore equivalent to לעשׂות שׂשׂ. At the same time, it may possibly be more correct to take צדק as the object of both verses, as Hofmann does in the sense of “those who let what is right be their joy, and their action also;” for though שׂוּשׂ (שׂישׂ) cannot be directly construed with the accusative of the object, as we have already observed at <reference osisRef="Isa.8.6">Isa 8:6</reference> and <reference osisRef="Isa.35.1">Isa 35:1</reference>, it may be indirectly, as in this passage and Isa 65:18. On <hi type="italic">pâga‛</hi>, “to come to meet,” in the sense of “coming to the help of,” see at <reference osisRef="Isa.47.3">Isa 47:3</reference>; it is here significantly interchanged with בּדרכיך of the minor clause <hi type="italic">bidrâkhekhâ</hi> <hi type="italic">yizkerūkhâ</hi>, “those who remember Thee in Thy ways” (for the syntax, compare <reference osisRef="Isa.1.5">Isa 1:5</reference> and <reference osisRef="Isa.26.16">Isa 26:16</reference>): “When such as love and do right, walking in Thy ways, remembered Thee (i.e., thanked Thee for grace received, and longed for fresh grace), Thou camest again and again to meet them as a friend.” <div eID="gen13667" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13668" type="x-p"/> But Israel appeared to have been given up without hope to the wrath of this very God. <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Isa.64.4">Isa 64:4</reference></hi> (5 <hi type="italic">b</hi>). <hi type="italic">“Behold, Thou, Thou art enraged, and we stood as sinners there; already have we been long in this state, and shall we be saved?”</hi> Instead of <hi type="italic">hēn</hi> <hi type="italic">‛attâh</hi> (the antithesis of now and formerly), the passage proceeds with <hi type="italic">hēn</hi> <hi type="italic">'attâh</hi>. There was no necessity for <hi type="italic">'attâh</hi> with <hi type="italic">qâtsaphtâ</hi>; so that it is used with special emphasis: <hi type="italic">“Behold, Thou, a God who so faithfully accepts His own people, hast broken out in wrath.”</hi> The following word ונּחטא cannot mean “and we have sinned,” but is a <hi type="italic">fut. consec.</hi>, and therefore must mean at least, “then we have sinned” (the sin inferred from the punishment). It is more correct, however, to take it, as in <reference osisRef="Gen.43.9">Gen 43:9</reference>, in the sense of, “Then we stand as sinners, as guilty persons:” the punishment has exhibited Israel before the world, and before itself, as what it really is (consequently the <hi type="italic">fut. consec.</hi> does not express the logical inference, but the practical consequence). As ונחטא has <hi type="italic">tsakeph</hi>, and therefore the accents at any rate preclude Shelling’s rendering, “and we have wandered in those ways from the very earliest times,” we must take the next two clauses as independent, if indeed בהם is to be understood as referring to בדרכיך. Stier only goes halfway towards this when he renders it, “And indeed in them (the ways of God, we sinned) from of old, and should we be helped?” This is forced, and yet not in accordance with the accents. Rosenmüller and Hahn quite satisfy this demand when they render it, “<hi type="italic">Tamen in viis tuis aeternitas ut salvemur</hi>;” but <hi type="italic">‛ōlâm</hi>, αἰών, in this sense of αἰωνιότης, is not scriptural. The rendering adopted by Besser, Grotius, and Starck is a better one: “(<hi type="italic">Si vero</hi>) <hi type="italic">in illis</hi> (<hi type="italic">viis</hi> <hi type="italic">tuis</hi>) <hi type="italic">perpetuo</hi> (<hi type="italic">mansissemus</hi>), <hi type="italic">tunc servati fuerimus</hi>” (if we had continued in Thy ways, then we should have been preserved). But there is no succession of tenses here, which could warrant us in taking ונוּשׁע as a <hi type="italic">paulo-post future;</hi> and Hofmann’s view is syntactically more correct, “In them (i.e., the ways of Jehovah) eternally, we shall find salvation, after the time is passed in which He has been angry and we have sinned” (or rather, been shown to be guilty). But we question the connection between בהם and רדכיך in any form. In our view the prayer suddenly takes a new turn from <hi type="italic">hēn</hi> (behold) onwards, just as it did with <hi type="italic">lū'</hi> (O that) in <reference osisRef="Isa.64.1">Isa 64:1</reference>; and רדכיך in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Isa.64.5">Isa 64:5</reference></hi> stands at the head of a subordinate clause. Hence בהם must refer back to ונחטא קצפת (“in Thine anger and in our sins,” Schegg). There is no necessity, however, to search for nouns to which to refer בּהם. It is rather to be taken as neuter, signifying “therein” (<reference osisRef="Ezek.33.18">Eze 33:18</reference>, cf., <reference osisRef="Ps.90.10">Psa 90:10</reference>), like עליהם, thereupon = thereby (<reference osisRef="Isa.38.16">Isa 38:16</reference>), בּהן therein (<reference osisRef="Isa.37.16">Isa 37:16</reference>), מהם thereout (<reference osisRef="Isa.30.6">Isa 30:6</reference>), therefrom (<reference osisRef="Isa.44.15">Isa 44:15</reference>). The idea suggested by such expressions as these is no doubt that of plurality (here a plurality of manifestations of wrath and of sins), but one which vanishes into the neuter idea of totality.
