Now we do justice both to the clause without a verb, which, being a logical <hi type="italic">copula</hi>, admits simply of a present <hi type="italic">sumus</hi>; and also to <hi type="italic">‛ōlâm</hi>, which is the accusative of duration, when we explain the sentence as meaning, “In this state we are and have been for a long time.” <hi type="italic">‛Olâm</hi> is used in other instances in these prophecies to denote the long continuance of the sate of punishment (see <reference osisRef="Isa.42.14">Isa 42:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.57.11">Isa 57:11</reference>), since it appeared to the exiles as an eternity (a whole aeon), and what lay beyond it as but a little while (<hi type="italic">mits‛âr</hi>, <reference osisRef="Isa.63.18">Isa 63:18</reference>). The following word ונוּשׁע needs no correction. There is no necessity to change it into ונּתע, as Ewald proposes, after the lxx καὶ ἐπλανήθημεν (“and we fell into wandering”), or what would correspond still more closely to the lxx (cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.46.8">Isa 46:8</reference>, פשׁעים, lxx πεπλανήμενοι), but is less appropriate here, into ונּפשׁע (“and we fell into apostasy”), the reading supported by Lowth and others. If it were necessary to alter the text at all, we might simply transpose the letters, and read וּנשׁוּע, “and cried for help.” But if we take it as a question, “And shall we experience salvation - find help?” there is nothing grammatically inadmissible in this (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.28.28">Isa 28:28</reference>), and psychologically it is commended by the state of mind depicted in <reference osisRef="Isa.40.27">Isa 40:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.59.10">Isa 59:10</reference>-12. Moreover, what follows attaches itself quite naturally to this.
entries.0664242fc37e98bdf6dae3ba81f751263687861b: <reference osisRef="Isa.64.5">Isa 64:5</reference> <div eID="gen13668" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13669" type="x-p"/> The people who ask the question in <reference osisRef="Isa.64.5">Isa 64:5</reference> do not regard themselves as worthy of redemption, as their self-righteousness has been so thoroughly put to shame. <hi type="italic">“We all became like the unclean thing, and all our virtues like a garment soiled with blood; and we all faded away together like the leaves; and our iniquities, like the storm they carried us away.”</hi> The whole nation is like one whom the law pronounces unclean, like a leper, who has to cry “<hi type="italic">tâmē</hi>, <hi type="italic">tâmē</hi> “as he goes along, that men may get out of his way (<reference osisRef="Lev.13.45">Lev 13:45</reference>). Doing right in all its manifold forms (<hi type="italic">tsedâqōth</hi>, like <reference osisRef="Isa.33.15">Isa 33:15</reference>, used elsewhere of the manifestations of divine righteousness), which once made Israel well-pleasing to God (<reference osisRef="Isa.1.21">Isa 1:21</reference>), has disappeared and become like a garment stained with menstruous discharge (cf., <reference osisRef="Ezek.36.17">Eze 36:17</reference>); (lxx ὡς ῥάκος ἀποκαθημένης = <hi type="italic">dâvâ</hi>, <reference osisRef="Isa.30.22">Isa 30:22</reference>; <hi type="italic">niddâh</hi>, <reference osisRef="Lam.1.17">Lam 1:17</reference>; <hi type="italic">temē'âh</hi>, <reference osisRef="Lev.15.33">Lev 15:33</reference>). <hi type="italic">‛Iddı̄m</hi> (used thus in the plural in the Talmud also) signifies the monthly period (<hi type="italic">menstrua</hi>). In the third figure, that of fading falling foliage, the form <hi type="italic">vannâbhel</hi> is not <hi type="italic">kal</hi> (= <hi type="italic">vannibbōl</hi> or <hi type="italic">vannibbal</hi>; Ewald, §232,<hi type="italic">b</hi>), which would be an impossibility according to the laws of inflexion; still less is it <hi type="italic">niphal</hi> = <hi type="italic">vanninnâbhel</hi> (which Kimchi suggests as an alternative); but certainly a <hi type="italic">hiphil</hi>. It is not, however, from <hi type="italic">nâbhēl</hi> = <hi type="italic">vannabbel</hi>, “with the reduplication dropped to express the idea of something gradual,” as Böttcher proposes (a new and arbitrary explanation in the place of one founded upon the simple laws of inflexion), but either from <hi type="italic">bâlal</hi> (compare the remarks on <hi type="italic">belı̄l</hi> in <reference osisRef="Isa.30.24">Isa 30:24</reference>, which hardly signifies “ripe barley” however), after the form ויּגל (from גּלל) ויּסך (from סכך), or from <hi type="italic">būl</hi>, after the form ויּקם, etc. In any case, therefore, it is a metaplastic formation, whether from <hi type="italic">bâlal</hi> or <hi type="italic">būl</hi> = <hi type="italic">nâbhēl</hi>, like ויּשׂר (in <reference osisRef="1Chr.20.3">1Ch 20:3</reference>, after the form ויּסר, from שּׂור = נשׂר, or after the form ויּרע, from שׂרר = נשׂר (compare the rabbinical explanation of the name of the month Bul from the falling of the leaves, in Buxtorf, <hi type="italic">Lex. talm.</hi> col. 271). The <hi type="italic">hiphil</hi> הבל or הביל is to be compared to האדים, to stream out red (= to be red); האריך, to make an extension (= to be long); השׁרישׁ, to strike root (= to root), etc., and signifies literally to produce a fading (= to fade away). In the fourth figure, עוננוּ (as it is also written in <reference osisRef="Isa.64.6">Isa 64:6</reference> according to correct codices) is a defective plural (as in <reference osisRef="Jer.14.7">Jer 14:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.28.18">Eze 28:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.9.13">Dan 9:13</reference>) for the more usual עונתינוּ (<reference osisRef="Isa.59.12">Isa 59:12</reference>). עון is the usual term applied to sin regarded as guilt, which produces punishment of itself. The people were robbed by their sins of all vital strength and energy, like dry leaves, which the guilt and punishment springing from sin carried off as a very easy prey.
entries.b5f7b1c50cfc354920a9865eab59293ca61a148c: <reference osisRef="Isa.64.6">Isa 64:6</reference> <div eID="gen13669" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13670" type="x-p"/> Universal forgetfulness of God was the consequence of this self-instigated departure from God. <hi type="italic">“And there was no one who called upon Thy name, who aroused himself to lay firm hold of Thee: for Thou hadst hidden Thy face from us, and didst melt us into the hand of our transgressions.”</hi> There was no one (see <reference osisRef="Isa.59.16">Isa 59:16</reference>) who had risen up in prayer and intercession out of this deep fall, or had shaken himself out of the sleep of security and lethargy of insensibility, to lay firm hold of Jehovah, i.e., not to let Him go till He blessed him and his people again. The curse of God pressed every one down; God had withdrawn His grace from them, and given them up to the consequences of their sins. The form ותּמוּגנוּ is not softened from the <hi type="italic">pilel</hi> ותּמגגנוּ, but is a <hi type="italic">kal</hi> like ויכוּננּוּ ekil  in <reference osisRef="Job.31.15">Job 31:15</reference> (which see), מוּג being used in a transitive sense, as <hi type="italic">kūn</hi> is there (cf., <hi type="italic">shūbh</hi>, <reference osisRef="Isa.52.8">Isa 52:8</reference>; <hi type="italic">mūsh</hi>, Zec 3:9). The lxx, Targ., and Syr. render it <hi type="italic">et tradidisti nos</hi>; but we cannot conclude from this with any certainty that they read ותּמגּננוּ, which Knobel follows Ewald in correcting into the incorrect form ותּמגּנּוּ. The prophet himself had the expression <hi type="italic">miggēn</hi> <hi type="italic">beyad</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gen.14.20">Gen 14:20</reference>, cf., <reference osisRef="Job.8.4">Job 8:4</reference>) in his mind, in the sense of <hi type="italic">liquefecisti nos in manum</hi>, equivalent to <hi type="italic">liquefecisti et tradidisti</hi> (παρέδωκας, <reference osisRef="Rom.1.28">Rom 1:28</reference>), from which it is evident that ביד is not a mere διά (lxx), but the “hand” of the transgressions is their destructive and damning power.
entries.119a4d71601bb750f4a8f41626c89c0436016f73: <reference osisRef="Isa.64.7-Isa.64.8">Isa 64:7-8</reference> <div eID="gen13670" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13671" type="x-p"/> This was the case when the measure of Israel’s sins had become full. They were carried into exile, where they sank deeper and deeper. The great mass of the people proved themselves to be really <hi type="italic">massa perdita</hi>, and perished among the heathen. But there were some, though a vanishingly small number, who humbled themselves under the mighty hand of God, and, when redemption could not be far off, wrestled in such prayers as these, that the nation might share it in its entirety, and if possible not one be left behind. With ועתּה the existing state of sin and punishment is placed among the things of the past, and the petition presented that the present moment of prayer may have all the significance of a turning-point in their history. <hi type="italic">“And now, O Jehovah, Thou art our Father: we are the clay, and Thou our Maker; and we are all the work of Thy hand. Be not extremely angry, O Jehovah, and remember not the transgression for ever! Behold, consider, we beseech Thee, we are all Thy people.”</hi> The state of things must change at last; for Israel is an image made by Jehovah; yea, more than this, Jehovah is the begetter of Israel, and loves Israel not merely as a sculptor, but as a father (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.45.9-Isa.45.10">Isa 45:9-10</reference>, and the unquestionable passage of Isaiah in <reference osisRef="Isa.29.16">Isa 29:16</reference>). Let Him then not be angry עד־מאד, “to the utmost measure” (cf., <reference osisRef="Ps.119.8">Psa 119:8</reference>), or if we paraphrase it according to the radical meaning of מד, “till the weight becomes intolerable.” Let Him not keep in mind the guilt for ever, to punish it; but, in consideration of the fact that Israel is the nation of His choice, let mercy take the place of justice. הן strengthens the petition in its own way (see <reference osisRef="Gen.30.34">Gen 30:34</reference>), just as נא does; and הבּיט signifies here, as elsewhere, to fix the eye upon anything. The object, in this instance, is the existing fact expressed in “we are all Thy people.” Hitzig is correct in regarding the repetition of “all of us” in this prayer as significant. The object throughout is to entreat that the whole nation may participate in the inheritance of the coming salvation, in order that the Exodus from Babylonia may resemble the Exodus from Egypt.
entries.222842bc7fef02c78598d74774b44628d8ed4367: <reference osisRef="Isa.64.9-Isa.64.11">Isa 64:9-11</reference> <div eID="gen13671" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13672" type="x-p"/> The re-erection of the ruins of the promised land requires the zeal of every one, and this state of ruin must not continue. It calls out the love and faithfulness of Jehovah. <hi type="italic">“The cities of Thy holiness have become a pasture-ground; Zion has become a pasture-ground, Jerusalem a desert. The house of our holiness and of our adorning, where our fathers praised Thee, is given up to the fire, and everything that was our delight given up to devastation. Wilt Thou restrain Thyself in spite of this, O Jehovah, be silent, and leave us to suffer the utmost?”</hi> Jerusalem by itself could not possibly be called “cities” (<hi type="italic">‛ârē</hi>), say with reference to the upper and lower cities (Vitringa). It is merely mentioned by name as the most prominent of the many cities which were all “holy cities,” inasmuch as the whole of Canaan was the land of Jehovah (<reference osisRef="Isa.14.25">Isa 14:25</reference>), and His holy territory (<reference osisRef="Ps.78.54">Psa 78:54</reference>). The word <hi type="italic">midbâr</hi> (pasture-land, heath, different from <hi type="italic">tsiyyâh</hi>, the pastureless desert, <reference osisRef="Isa.35.1">Isa 35:1</reference>) is repeated, for the purpose of showing that the same fate had fallen upon Zion-Jerusalem as upon the rest of the cities of the land. The climax of the terrible calamity was the fact, that the temple had also fallen a prey to the burning of the fire (compare for the fact, <reference osisRef="Jer.52.13">Jer 52:13</reference>). The people call it “house of our holiness and of our glory.” Jehovah’s <hi type="italic">qōdesh</hi> and <hi type="italic">tiph'ereth</hi> have, as it were, transplanted heaven to earth in the temple (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.63.15">Isa 63:15</reference> with <reference osisRef="Isa.60.7">Isa 60:7</reference>); and this earthly dwelling-place of God is Israel’s possession, and therefore Israel’s <hi type="italic">qōdesh</hi> and <hi type="italic">tiph'ereth</hi>. The relative clause describes what sublime historical reminiscences are attached to the temple: אשׁר is equivalent to שׁם אשׁר, as in <reference osisRef="Gen.39.20">Gen 39:20</reference>; Num 20:13 (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.84.4">Psa 84:4</reference>), <reference osisRef="Deut.8.15">Deu 8:15</reference>, etc. הללּך has <hi type="italic">chateph</hi>-<hi type="italic">pathach</hi>, into which, as a rule, the vocal sheva under the first of two similar letters is changed. <hi type="italic">Machămaddēnū</hi> (our delights) may possibly include favourite places, ornamental buildings, and pleasure grounds; but the parallel leads us rather to think primarily of things associated with the worship of God, in which the people found a holy delight. כל, contrary to the usual custom, is here followed by the singular of the predicate, as in <reference osisRef="Prov.16.2">Pro 16:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.31.15">Eze 31:15</reference> (cf., <reference osisRef="Gen.9.29">Gen 9:29</reference>). Will Jehovah still put restraint upon Himself, and cause His merciful love to keep silence, על־זאת, with such a state of things as this, or notwithstanding this state of things (<reference osisRef="Job.10.7">Job 10:7</reference>)? <hi type="italic">On</hi> התאפּק, see <reference osisRef="Isa.63.15">Isa 63:15</reference>; Isa 42:14. The suffering would indeed increase עד־מאד (to the utmost), if it caused the destruction of Israel, or should not be followed at last by Israel’s restoration. Jehovah’s compassion cannot any longer thus forcibly restrain itself; it must break forth, like Joseph’s tears in the recognition scene (<reference osisRef="Gen.45.1">Gen 45:1</reference>).  <chapter eID="Isa.64"/> <div eID="gen13672" type="x-p"/>
